e.t: This noun means “pride; boastfulness”—an attitude of self-importance expressed through boasting or exalting oneself. It describes an inward disposition rather than a physical object or action. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs four times, including passages in Job, Isaiah, Jeremiah, and Baruch. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage, but its central idea remains proud self-exaltation.

This word means “buy”: to obtain something by paying for it. It is a verb describing an action in ordinary commerce, such as acquiring food or other goods. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek Jewish writings represented here, it occurs 22 times, showing a consistent meaning across passages rather than a rare or specialized sense. The word appears in Genesis, Deuteronomy, and other books, where the surrounding passage determines what is being purchased and why. Its basic idea remains the act of obtaining something through purchase.

Aziēl, also rendered Azil, is a personal name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, this name appears once, in Ezra 8:5. The name identifies the individual mentioned there, while the surrounding verse supplies the person’s specific role or relationship. By itself, the name does not establish an additional spiritual or symbolic meaning.

Akoun, also rendered “Akun,” is a proper name identifying a particular person. It is not a general description or action word, but a personal name preserved in the Greek Old Testament. This name occurs once in the Greek Old Testament corpus, at 1 Chronicles 3:24. Its precise significance in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the word itself functions as the name of an individual rather than as a term describing a quality, event, or command.

This word means “unmixed,” describing something kept pure rather than combined with another substance. It can function as an adjective or as a noun, depending on how the sentence uses it. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs three times: in Psalms, Jeremiah, and 3 Maccabees. Its basic idea remains consistent wherever it appears: something is presented without mixture or dilution. The surrounding verse determines what particular thing is being described.

This verb means “grind”: to crush or break something into smaller particles by rubbing or pressing it. It describes an action rather than an object, so it can be rendered according to the sentence as someone grinding or something being ground. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs four times, in Numbers, Judges, and Ecclesiastes. Its appearances include the grinding of food and the work associated with a mill, but the surrounding verse determines the precise action being described.

This adjective describes something salty or briny—having the character or taste of salt. It is a descriptive word rather than a name for salt itself, so it identifies the quality of what it modifies. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Jeremiah 17:6. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and context, but its ordinary meaning is the salty or briny quality of something.

Amram is a personal name, referring to a man named Amram rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, the name appears four times, all within the Old Testament books represented here. It is rendered consistently as “Amram,” so its role is to identify a particular person. The name itself does not provide enough information to state its meaning or explain the person’s actions without the surrounding verse and passage.

Anath is a proper name, rendered simply as “Anath.” It functions as a specific name rather than a common word describing an object, action, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament corpus, it occurs twice: once in Joshua and once in Judges. The name itself does not provide a broader descriptive meaning, so its precise reference in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and context.

This verb means to “act lawlessly”—to behave in a way that disregards or violates lawful instruction. It describes conduct rather than a person or object. In the Greek Old Testament and deuterocanonical writings, it occurs 42 times, showing repeated use for wrongdoing understood as lawless behavior. Its exact force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea remains acting contrary to what is rightly commanded.

This verb means “estrange”: to make someone or something distant, separated, or no longer closely connected. It describes a change in relationship rather than a physical action alone. In the Greek LXX, it occurs 11 times across the Old Testament and Deuterocanonical books, so its basic sense is consistent while the surrounding context determines what has become distant or separated. The word appears in passages from Joshua, Job, Psalms, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, Hosea, and 3 Maccabees.

This adjective describes someone or something as “untried” or “unacquainted with” something. It points to a lack of experience, familiarity, or firsthand knowledge. In the Septuagint corpus, it appears four times across Numbers, Jeremiah, Zechariah, and Wisdom. Its exact force—whether emphasizing inexperience or unfamiliarity—depends on the sentence in which it occurs, but its central idea remains that something has not been tested, experienced, or known.

This adjective describes something done or obtained “without toil,” meaning without laborious effort or strenuous work. It presents the absence of toil as the defining quality of a person, action, or result. The word appears once in the Greek LXX corpus, in 4 Maccabees 11:26, so its precise force there depends on the surrounding verse and passage. Its central idea remains straightforward: what is described does not involve the hard work normally associated with toil.

This verb means to give a fifth part, describing the act of assigning or handing over one portion out of five. It expresses a specific quantity rather than a general gift or offering. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, both times in Genesis, so its known use is focused and limited. The word itself identifies what is given by its proportion: a fifth part. Its exact force in any sentence depends on what is being divided or assigned there.

This Greek LXX noun refers to Arcturus, also rendered “Bear.” It is the name of a heavenly object rather than a description of a person, action, or quality. The word occurs once in the Greek Old Testament represented here, at Job 9:9. Its precise significance in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its ordinary lexical meaning is the named object Arcturus, with “Bear” supplied as the related rendering. The word’s identity and meaning are clear even though it appears only once in this corpus.

This Greek LXX noun means “raising,” referring to the act or process of raising something or someone. It names an action rather than describing a person or object. The word occurs 10 times across 9 Old Testament verses in the Greek Septuagint, including passages in Samuel, Kings, and Psalms. Its precise emphasis—what is being raised and why—depends on the surrounding verse, but its central idea remains the act of raising.

Astarothi is a proper name, rendered in the gloss as “Astarōthi; Astarothi.” It identifies a particular person or named entity rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament corpus, this name occurs only once, at 1 Chronicles 11:44. The available information does not include the verse text or surrounding passage, so the name’s specific identification there cannot be explained further here. Its basic meaning is therefore its function as a personal or proper name: Astarothi.

This adverb means “without any possibility of escape”: it describes an action, situation, or outcome that cannot be avoided or escaped. It presents something as unavoidable rather than merely difficult or unlikely. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, in 3 Maccabees 7:9. The precise force of the word in that sentence depends on its surrounding context, but its basic meaning remains the certainty that no escape is possible.

Balaennōn is a proper name, rendered as “Balaennōn” or “Valaennon.” It identifies a person rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs four times: twice in Genesis and twice in 1 Chronicles. The name appears in genealogical or historical listings, but the available wording does not provide further meaning for the name itself. Its precise reference is determined by the surrounding passage in each occurrence.

Baraga, also rendered Varaga, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a person in the Greek Old Testament and occurs once, in 1 Chronicles 7:23. Because the surrounding verse text is not included here, the name’s particular role in that passage cannot be described further. Its meaning is therefore best stated as the personal name “Baraga; Varaga,” with the spelling reflecting the form preserved in this Greek text.

This Greek LXX verb means “bewitch”: it describes the act of bewitching someone. As a verb, it expresses what a person does rather than naming a person, object, or general condition. It occurs four times in the Greek LXX corpus, twice in Deuteronomy and twice in Sirach. The references are Deuteronomy 28:54 and 28:56, and Sirach 14:6 and 14:8. The surrounding verse context is needed to explain the particular force of the word in each passage.

This verb means to look at something or to see it. It describes the act of directing one’s sight toward a person, object, or scene, and can be used for ordinary visual perception. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs 122 times, showing that it is a normal and widely used word for seeing or looking. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

Garabeththi, also rendered Garaveththi, is a proper name rather than a common word describing an object, action, or quality. It identifies a person or named figure in the Greek Old Testament tradition. This name occurs once in the Greek text, at 1 Chronicles 11:32. Without the surrounding verse text, Scripture does not provide enough information here to explain the person’s role or the significance of the name beyond its identification as a proper name.

This noun means “tillage” or “agriculture,” referring to the cultivation of land and the work involved in producing crops. It describes farming as a practical activity rather than a person or tool. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs three times: once in Genesis and twice in deuterocanonical writings. Its precise emphasis in any particular verse depends on the surrounding context.

This Greek LXX word is a conjunction or particle meaning “though” or “while.” It links words or clauses, helping express a relationship between what is being said and what follows. Its precise force depends on the surrounding sentence, but its normal use marks a connection such as concession or time. It occurs 4,597 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, showing that it is a common linking word rather than a term naming a person, object, or action.

This verb means “lord”: it describes acting as lord or exercising lordship. It expresses the position or action of one who rules or holds authority over others. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented in this LXX corpus, it occurs 15 times, so its central idea is consistent but its precise force depends on the sentence where it appears. It is distinct from a noun naming a lord; it describes what a lord does or how lordship is exercised.

This verb means “cry out”: to call aloud or raise one’s voice. It describes an audible act of speaking or calling rather than a person, object, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, showing a focused but straightforward use. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding words and situation, but the central idea remains an outward, audible cry. The word appears in Genesis 45:16 and Leviticus 25:10.

gl: set the warp in the loom; begin the web
d: set the warp in the loom; begin the web

e.t: This Greek LXX verb means “set the warp in the loom; begin the web.” It describes starting the process of preparing threads so weaving can begin. The word occurs once in the Greek Old Testament represented here, at Isaiah 19:10. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic picture is clear: arranging the warp and initiating the work of making cloth. It is therefore a practical action word connected with the first stage of weaving.

This Greek LXX verb means “twist” or “divert”: it describes turning something away from a straight, proper, or intended course. It can refer to a literal turning or to the bending of conduct, direction, or judgment. The word appears 33 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, so its central idea is used across several kinds of passages rather than being limited to one setting. Its precise force in any verse depends on what is being turned or diverted. [p03:word:lxx:L703592:identity] [p03:word:lxx:L703592:occurrences]

This Greek LXX verb means “deteriorate” or “ruin.” It describes something becoming spoiled, damaged, or brought into a ruined condition, and it can also express the action of ruining something. The word appears 66 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books represented in this corpus, so it is used for more than one kind of damage or decline. Its exact force—whether something deteriorates or is ruined by another—depends on the sentence and surrounding passage.

δικάζω means “judge; give judgment on.” As a verb, it describes the act of making a judgment or rendering a decision concerning someone or something. In the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books represented here, it occurs 23 times, so it is a recurring word for judging rather than a rare expression. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

This Greek LXX verb means “think”: it describes the act of holding a thought or view in the mind. As a verb, it expresses what someone thinks rather than naming a person, object, or quality. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 2 Maccabees 6:13. The surrounding verse text is needed to explain what thought is expressed there; the word itself supplies the basic idea of thinking.

“Long about” is a verb describing longing in relation to something. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears three times, all in Proverbs, so its meaning is best kept focused on this expression of longing rather than broadened into an unrelated idea. The word identifies an action or state of longing, while the surrounding sentence determines what is being longed for. It occurs in Proverbs 9:18, 10:28, and 23:30.

Ethnan is a personal name, referring to an individual rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in 1 Chronicles 4:7. The available wording identifies the person by name, but without the verse text and surrounding passage, no further personal description or significance can be established from this word alone. Its ordinary function is simply to identify Ethnan as a named person.

This word means “image”: a likeness or representation of something. It is a noun used for an image as an identifiable object or representation. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears 40 times, including passages in Genesis, Deuteronomy, Isaiah, and Ezekiel. Its basic meaning can describe an image without, by itself, explaining whether that image is honored, forbidden, symbolic, or merely descriptive; the surrounding passage determines that role.

The verb means “cut out; cut off.” It describes removing something by cutting, whether an object is separated from its place or something is eliminated. In the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical writings, it appears 41 times, so its basic sense is established across repeated uses rather than being limited to one passage. The exact object being removed—and whether the wording emphasizes separation or elimination—comes from the surrounding verse. It is a verb, expressing an action rather than naming a person or thing.

This Greek LXX verb means “saw out”: to cut something out by sawing. It describes an action rather than an object, naming the work of removing or shaping something through sawing. The word occurs twice in the Greek LXX corpus, once in Proverbs and once in Wisdom. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse, but its basic meaning remains the act of sawing something out.

Elami is a proper name, rendered as “Elami.” It identifies a particular named entity rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs once, at 1 Kings 12:24. Because the verse text and surrounding context are not available here, the name’s specific referent in that passage cannot be identified more precisely from this word alone.

Emmōth, also rendered Emmoth, is a proper name identifying a particular named entity rather than describing a general action, quality, or object. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, at 2 Chronicles 11:20. The available information preserves the name itself but does not identify whether the named entity is a person, place, or something else. Its precise reference is therefore understood from the surrounding verse and passage.

gl: one who is in the way; troubler
d: one who is in the way; troubler

e.t: This noun describes someone who gets in the way or causes trouble—a “troubler.” It refers to a person whose presence or actions hinder others rather than help them. The word appears once in the Greek Old Testament, at 1 Chronicles 2:7. Since the surrounding verse text is not included here, the word’s precise force in that passage must be understood from its context. Its basic sense remains clear: a person who obstructs, interferes, or creates difficulty for others.

This Greek verb means “draw out”: to pull or bring something outward from where it is. It can describe physically extracting something, but the exact object and force depend on the surrounding sentence. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings, it appears five times, including passages in Genesis, Job, Proverbs, and 3 Maccabees. Its central idea remains movement from within or away from a place, rather than merely touching or moving something nearby.

This noun means “insurrection”: an organized rising against established authority. It names the act or condition of rebellion rather than a person who rebels. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at 2 Kings 3:4. The word’s basic sense is therefore a public uprising or revolt, while the surrounding verse determines the precise force of the term in that passage. [p03:word:lxx:L705019:identity] [p03:word:lxx:L705019:occurrences] [p01:word:lxx:L705019:reference:0]

This verb means to pull something onto someone or to put something on them. It describes an action of placing or mounting, depending on what is being moved or who receives it. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 10 times across 9 verses, so its basic sense is repeated in several settings rather than belonging to one isolated passage. The precise force in any verse depends on the surrounding words and the object involved.

This Greek LXX noun means “aid”—help given to support someone or something in need. It describes assistance rather than the person or thing receiving help. The word occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, in Wisdom 13:18, so its broader range cannot be established from repeated uses. Its basic sense remains straightforward: practical or sustaining help provided for support. The surrounding verse is needed to determine exactly how that idea functions in its context.

This verb means to add strength to something or someone—to strengthen. It describes an action that makes another person, thing, or condition stronger, firmer, or better able to continue. In the Greek Old Testament tradition represented here, it occurs once, in 2 Maccabees 11:9. The basic sense is direct: strength is supplied or increased. The surrounding passage is needed to determine exactly what is being strengthened in that occurrence, but the word itself expresses the act of giving added strength.

Esrōm, also rendered Ezrom, is a proper name for a person in the Greek Old Testament. It functions as a personal name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. The name occurs three times in the Greek Old Testament, appearing twice in Ruth and once in 1 Kings. Without the surrounding verse text, the name itself identifies the person but does not supply further information about his role or significance in each passage.

This adjective describes someone as “very merciful,” emphasizing abundant compassion and readiness to show mercy. It presents mercy as especially great rather than limited or occasional. In the Greek Old Testament, this word occurs once, in Psalm 98:8. Its precise force in that verse belongs with the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning is clear: it characterizes a person as exceptionally compassionate and merciful.

This Greek LXX verb means “orderly; behave well.” It describes acting in a proper, disciplined, and well-arranged way rather than behaving carelessly or disruptively. As a verb, it expresses the action of conducting oneself properly. It occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, in 2 Maccabees 4:27. The precise force of the word in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central meaning is orderly behavior.

Ērem, also rendered Irem, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, in Ezra 2:39, identifying a person or group by name. The available wording establishes the name itself, but the surrounding verse text is needed to determine precisely whom it identifies there. Its normal meaning is therefore the personal or group name “Ērem” or “Irem.”

Thanak is a proper name, identifying a particular person or place rather than expressing a general idea, action, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament tradition represented here, it appears once, at Judges 1:27. The name itself does not describe a broader concept or provide a separate definition; its specific reference must be understood from the surrounding verse and passage. Thanak remains a distinct Greek LXX word entity, not a Greek New Testament word.

This noun means “divinity,” referring to the quality or reality of being divine. It speaks of what belongs to God or expresses divine nature, rather than naming a particular person or action. In the Greek Old Testament, this word occurs once, in Wisdom 18:9. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and paragraph, but its central meaning remains the divine nature or character. The word is therefore a concise expression for divinity within this Greek Old Testament corpus.

Thermai, also called Therme, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a named place or person in the Greek Old Testament, but the available lexical information does not specify which kind of named entity it is. This name occurs once in the LXX, at 1 Kings 2:46. Its precise referent must therefore be determined from that passage’s surrounding text.

This noun describes someone who is “bearing a shield.” It refers to a person characterized by carrying a shield, rather than to the shield itself or to an action apart from that person. In the Greek LXX, it occurs once, at 1 Chronicles 12:25. The word therefore names a person according to what he carries. Its precise significance in that verse depends on the surrounding passage.

Iaōs, also written Iaos, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It functions as a name in the Greek Septuagint text. This name occurs once in the LXX corpus, at 1 Chronicles 8:10. The name itself supplies no further meaning or description in the available lexical information, so its significance in that passage must come from the surrounding verse and context.

This Greek LXX noun means “idea; appearance,” referring either to a thought or concept, or to the way something looks. It can therefore describe what is held in the mind or what is presented to the eyes. The word occurs five times in the Greek LXX corpus, in both Old Testament and deuterocanonical writings. Its precise sense in any particular verse depends on whether the surrounding passage is speaking about an inward concept or an outward appearance.

Ierobaal, also rendered Ierovaal, is a personal name used in the Greek Septuagint. It identifies a person rather than describing an object, action, or quality. The name occurs 15 times in the Old Testament Greek corpus, appearing most often in Judges and also in 1 Samuel, 2 Samuel, and Hosea. Its precise significance in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic function remains that of a personal name.

This Greek LXX verb means “make to sit down.” It describes causing a person or group to take a seated position, rather than sitting by their own choice. The word occurs three times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, including 2 Maccabees, 3 Maccabees, and the Epistle of Jeremiah. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on who is being seated and why, but its central idea is placing or settling someone in a sitting position.

This Greek LXX verb means to veil: to cover something with a veil or place it behind a covering. It describes an action rather than a person or object. The word appears 25 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical material, with uses extending across Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, and Sirach. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on what is being covered and the surrounding sentence.

This verb means to “return home”—to go back to one’s home or place of residence. It describes movement toward home rather than simply traveling somewhere. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs twice, in 2 Maccabees and 3 Maccabees. Its exact force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and situation, but the central idea remains going back home. The word therefore presents home as the destination of the person or people who are leaving and returning.

This verb means to treat someone spitefully—to act toward them with deliberate malice or contempt. It describes hostile treatment rather than a neutral action. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at Zechariah 12:10. The word’s precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic sense is clear: treating another person in a spiteful, hurtful way.

This Greek LXX verb means “gore; butt with horns.” It describes the action of a horned animal striking or thrusting with its horns. The word occurs 12 times in the Greek Old Testament, including laws concerning an ox that attacks people or another animal, and descriptions involving horns. Its central sense is physical aggression carried out with horns, while the exact force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

Kison is a proper name, rendered “Kisōn” or “Kison.” It identifies a named person, place, or other entity in the Greek Old Testament, but the available word-level information does not specify which kind. The name occurs eight times in seven Old Testament verses, from Joshua through Psalms. Its precise reference in any particular verse must be understood from that verse’s surrounding passage.

The word is the proper name “Knidos,” also given as “Knithos.” It identifies a named entity rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 1 Maccabees 15:23. Without the surrounding verse text, the evidence establishes the name and its spelling variants but does not provide further contextual significance. Its precise reference in that passage must therefore be understood from the verse and its surrounding context.

This LXX adjective means “just the one,” pointing to a single person or thing rather than others. It functions as a describing word, adding the sense of singularity or exclusiveness to the noun it modifies. The word occurs 10 times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented in this LXX corpus, including Judges, Ruth, Psalms, Proverbs, and Sirach. Its exact force in any verse depends on the noun and surrounding sentence.

This Greek LXX noun means “pit,” referring to a hollow or deep opening in the ground. It can describe a place into which someone or something may fall, be thrown, or remain, and it may also refer to a waterless or otherwise empty underground cavity. The word occurs 77 times in the Greek Old Testament and Deuterocanonical books, so it is a recurring term for this kind of physical place. Its precise force in any passage depends on the surrounding context.

Logos is a noun meaning “word” or “log.” It names a word within a sentence or passage, while the surrounding context determines what that word refers to. In the Greek Old Testament, logos appears 1,130 times, making it a very common term. Its basic meaning remains broad rather than pointing to one specific subject or kind of message. It occurs throughout the Old Testament and in deuterocanonical Greek writings.

This word describes speech or behavior that reviles—expressing abusive contempt toward someone. As an adjective, it identifies a person or action marked by insulting, scornful language rather than respectful speech. It occurs three times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here: twice in Proverbs and once in Sirach. Its basic sense remains focused on verbal abuse or contempt, while the surrounding verse determines exactly who is being described and how the reviling is expressed.

This noun refers to a medicinal plaster or an emollient—a soothing substance applied to the body. It describes a practical treatment intended to soften, cover, or help heal an injury or affected area. The word appears three times in the Greek Old Testament and related Wisdom literature, including Isaiah, Ezekiel, and Wisdom. Its precise force in any individual passage depends on the surrounding context, but its central sense remains a healing or soothing application.

This noun means the ceiling of a room—the overhead surface that forms the top or covering of an interior space. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears four times, all in 1 Kings, in descriptions involving the construction and furnishings of the temple and royal buildings. Its meaning is concrete and architectural, referring to a room’s upper covering rather than to the roof of an entire building. The word is found in 1 Kings 6:5, 7:9, and 7:41.

This word describes someone who is “lightly armed,” referring to a person equipped with relatively light weapons or protection. It can function as an adjective describing a person or group, or as a noun referring to such a lightly equipped person. In the Greek Old Testament represented by this LXX entity, it occurs ten times across seven verses. Its precise force in a particular passage depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea remains a person who is lightly armed.

This noun means “nose” or “snout,” referring to the projecting part of a person’s or animal’s face. It is a concrete bodily term rather than an abstract idea. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs ten times across ten verses, including passages from Numbers, 2 Kings, Job, Proverbs, Ezekiel, and other books. The word can therefore describe either a human nose or an animal’s snout, with the surrounding verse determining which is intended. Its precise reference in any particular passage depends on the immediate context.

Nachaligaas is a proper name, identifying a named individual rather than describing an action, quality, or object. It functions simply as a personal designation. In the Greek Old Testament (the Septuagint), it occurs once, at 1 Chronicles 11:32. It is also rendered Nakhaligaas. The available meaning is limited to the name itself, so its precise role in that passage must be understood from the surrounding verse and passage, not from the name alone.

This adverb means “according to the law” or “legitimately.” It describes an action or situation as being in proper agreement with law, rather than outside lawful order. In the LXX, it occurs once, at Proverbs 31:28, so its established meaning is clear even though the available record does not include the verse text or surrounding context. The word tells the reader how something is done or regarded: in a lawful, proper, or legitimate way.

This noun refers to a person who drinks wine. It describes someone by association with wine-drinking rather than naming the drink itself. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Proverbs 23:20. The word’s basic meaning is direct: a wine-drinker is a person characterized by drinking wine. Its precise force in that verse is understood from the surrounding wording and passage, but the word itself identifies the person as a wine-drinker.

This adjective describes someone or something as passionate—marked by strong feeling or intense ardor. It functions as a descriptive word, identifying a person or thing characterized by passion rather than merely mentioning an action. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs four times, appearing once in Psalms and three times in Proverbs. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

This word is a proper name, rendered “Oul” or “Ul,” rather than a term describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears only once, in Genesis 10:23, identifying a named figure in the genealogy recorded there. Because the verse text is not included here, the name’s specific identity and role must be understood from that surrounding passage.

Pamphylia is the name of a place, specifically a region known by that name. In this Greek LXX entry, the word functions as a proper noun rather than describing an action, quality, or person. It occurs once in the deuterocanonical corpus, at 1 Maccabees 15:23. The lexical meaning identifies the place as “Pamphylia,” also rendered “Pamfilia.” Its precise significance in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, which is not included here.

This adjective describes something stimulating—something that prompts, encourages, or stirs a response. It identifies a quality rather than an action or person, so its precise force depends on the noun or situation it describes. In the Greek Old Testament, this word occurs once, in Zechariah 1:13. The available lexical sense is clear, while the verse’s particular emphasis must be understood from its surrounding passage. [p03:word:lxx:L710048:identity] [p03:word:lxx:L710048:occurrences] [p01:word:lxx:L710048:reference:0]

This verb describes speaking candidly or acting with confidence. It can express openness in what a person says and assurance in how a person approaches a matter. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs five times, appearing in Job, Psalms, Proverbs, and Sirach. Its precise force in any one passage depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea is straightforward, confident openness rather than hesitation or concealment.

This Greek LXX adjective means “broad” and can describe a street or other wide space. It presents the idea of breadth rather than narrowness. The word occurs 38 times in the Greek Old Testament and related LXX books, appearing in descriptions of physical spaces and streets. Its exact force in a particular verse depends on what it describes there, but its central idea remains something broad, wide, or associated with a street.

This noun means “shepherd,” a person who cares for and guides sheep. It normally identifies someone whose work involves tending a flock. In the Greek Old Testament, the word occurs 80 times, appearing across historical, poetic, and prophetic books. Its basic meaning remains the same whether it describes an individual shepherd or shepherds as a group. The word can therefore refer simply to an occupation or role, while the surrounding passage determines any further significance. It is found from Genesis through Song of Songs in the LXX corpus.

This adjective describes something connected with battle or warfare—something martial, combat-related, or used in a fighting setting. Its basic meaning is “of battle.” In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs 13 times, showing that it can describe people, equipment, or circumstances associated with armed conflict. The surrounding sentence determines exactly what battle-related thing it describes, but the central idea remains clear: it belongs to, concerns, or serves warfare.

This Greek LXX noun refers to an emerald or to a light-green color. It can identify the green appearance associated with an emerald, rather than describing an action or relationship. The word occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, at Genesis 2:12. Without the verse text, its precise descriptive force in that passage cannot be expanded beyond this basic meaning.

“Opening” refers to the beginning or introductory part of something. As a noun, this word names what comes first, serving as an entry into what follows rather than describing the whole message or event. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears three times, all in Job: Job 25:2, Job 27:1, and Job 29:1. Its precise force in any one passage depends on the surrounding verse and speech.

This Greek LXX verb means “set on fire beside.” It describes the act of placing fire beside something so that it is ignited, rather than naming the fire itself. The word is a verb and occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, at Exodus 22:5. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning is an action of setting something alight alongside another thing.

This adjective means “from Ptolemy,” identifying something as connected with or originating from a person named Ptolemy. It functions as a describing word rather than naming an action or quality by itself. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 3 Maccabees 1:2. The surrounding verse is needed to know exactly what it describes there, but its basic meaning remains a reference to Ptolemy or to something associated with him.

This adjective describes something that is clear, plain, or easy to understand. It can characterize words, statements, or matters presented without obscurity, so the reader can recognize their meaning directly. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs four times, each in a different verse. Its basic sense remains focused on clarity rather than complexity or hiddenness. The exact force in any particular passage depends on the surrounding wording, but the central idea is that what is described is made plain and readily understood.

This word means “of iron,” describing something made from or associated with the hard metal iron. It can function as a noun when referring to iron itself and as an adjective when describing an iron object or feature. In the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical writings, it occurs 36 times, showing a normal material sense rather than an abstract idea. It appears in passages throughout books such as Deuteronomy, Daniel, Jeremiah, Psalms, and 4 Maccabees. Its exact force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence.

This word is a proper name rendered as “Soēnē” or “Sini.” It identifies a named entity rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament (LXX), it occurs once, in Isaiah 43:3. As a name, its meaning is chiefly its identification of the person, place, or entity named in that passage; the lexical information does not specify which kind. Its precise reference therefore belongs to the verse context.

In the Greek Old Testament, this verb describes something as rare or scarce—something not readily found or available. It can refer to limited presence or supply rather than abundance. The word occurs three times in the Greek Old Testament, so it expresses a specific condition of lack or uncommonness, not a broad range of unrelated ideas. Its exact force in any verse depends on what the surrounding passage identifies as rare or scarce.

This Greek LXX verb means to aim—to direct one’s purpose or effort toward something. It describes intentional movement toward a goal rather than accidental action. The word occurs twice in the deuterocanonical Greek writings represented here, once in Wisdom and once in 2 Maccabees. Its basic sense remains focused and purposeful: a person aims at an objective, whether the objective is expressed directly or understood from the surrounding sentence. The exact force in either occurrence depends on the verse’s context, but the central idea is deliberate direction toward a desired end.

This LXX Greek verb means to carry something or someone around along with another. It describes an action of bearing or moving together, with the idea that one thing accompanies another rather than being carried alone. The word appears five times in the LXX corpus, in Proverbs, Sirach, and 2 and 3 Maccabees. Its exact force in any particular verse depends on what is being carried and who or what accompanies it.

This verb describes being “privy to” something—that is, being aware of it or having knowledge of it. It expresses a person’s relationship to information, not an action performed on an object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, both times in Job, showing a focused use rather than a broad range of applications. Its precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding passage.

Sōbal, also rendered Soval, is a personal name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it identifies people in genealogical passages. It occurs seven times, in Genesis and 1 Chronicles, where the surrounding names distinguish the individuals being listed. The name itself does not provide a broader teaching or concept apart from identifying those persons.

This Greek LXX adverb means “more quickly” or “quicker,” describing an action done with greater speed than another action or point of comparison. It functions as a comparative word, so it expresses increased rapidity rather than simply stating that something happens quickly. The word occurs twice in the deuterocanonical Greek corpus, in Wisdom and 1 Maccabees. Its exact force in either passage depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central meaning remains a comparison of speed.

Timotheos is a proper name used to identify a person. It functions as a personal name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs 18 times, all in the deuterocanonical books of 1 and 2 Maccabees. The name appears across these historical narratives, but its precise significance in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This noun means “bone-crusher,” referring to a person or thing associated with crushing bones. It appears once in the Greek LXX corpus, at 4 Maccabees 8:13. The word therefore names a distinct agent or implement by its crushing action, rather than describing a general quality. Without the verse text, the exact contextual force cannot be stated beyond this basic meaning.

Phalletia is a proper name, also given as “Falletia.” It identifies a person or named individual rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Septuagint corpus, this name occurs once, in 1 Chronicles 3:21. The name itself supplies identification, while the surrounding verse and genealogy determine which individual is being named there. Its precise role in that verse therefore depends on the passage context.

This verb means that something becomes visible or appears. It describes coming into view rather than simply existing unseen, so it focuses on the act of being seen. In the LXX corpus, it occurs twice, once in Wisdom and once in Sirach. Its basic sense is appearing, while the precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding sentence and context.

Phedeia, also rendered Fethia, is a personal name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in 2 Kings 23:36. Its role is to identify a person, while the surrounding verse supplies the particular information associated with that person. The name itself does not provide a broader teaching or concept apart from its use as a personal designation.

Chereththi, also rendered Khereththi, is a proper name or designation rather than a general action, quality, or object. It identifies the Chereththi in the Greek Old Testament wording. The term occurs six times in the LXX, in passages from 2 Samuel, 1 Kings, and 1 Chronicles. Its exact reference in any particular verse must be understood from that passage’s surrounding text, but the word itself functions as a named designation, not as a description with a broader meaning.

This noun means “use,” referring to the usefulness or practical value something has. It can describe whether a person, action, or thing serves a worthwhile purpose. In the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, it occurs 13 times, so its central idea is consistent while the surrounding passage determines what is being considered useful. The word appears across books including 2 Samuel, Job, Psalms, Isaiah, Jeremiah, Sirach, and 2 Maccabees. Its precise force in any verse depends on the subject and sentence around it.
